body.p: Avram’s (Abram’s) Journey to Kena’an (Canaan)
Avram, Saray (Sarai), and Lot traveled from Ur of the Kasdim (Chaldeans) by way of Haran.
Ararat Mountains
These mountains are located in present-day Turkey, near the Russian border.
Cities of Refuge
Six cities were designated as cities of refuge. They were spaced throughout the land and protected those who had accidentally committed a crime or who were awaiting trial.

item.name: CreteanIslandintheMediterranean
item.title: Crete, an Island in the Mediterranean

body.p: Kraitai (Crete), an Island in the Mediterranean

Tradition says that after Paulos (Paul) was released from prison in Romai (Rome) (before his second and final Roman imprisonment), he and Titos (Titus) traveled together for a while. They stopped in Kraitai, and when it was time for Paulos to go, he left Titos behind to help the churches there.
Damesek (Damascus)

The apostle Paulos (Paul) had his famous conversion experience on his way to Damesek. Paulos (then called Sha’ul (Saul)) traveled 150 miles (241.4 kilometers) from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to Damesek in order to bring Christians back in chains. But as he neared the ancient city, he discovered that God had other plans for him (Acts 9:15).
David Flees from Sha’ul (Saul)

David and his men attacked the Pelishtim (Philistines) at Ke’ilah (Keilah) from the forest of Heret (Hereth). Sha’ul came from Giveah (Gibeah) to attack David, but David escaped into the wilderness of Zif (Ziph). At Horesh he met Yonatan (Jonathan), who encouraged him. Then he fled into the wilderness of Maeon (Maon) and into the strongholds of Eyn-Gedi (En-gedi).
Derbai (Derbe)
After Paulos (Paul) was stoned in Lustra (Lystra), he and Barnabas traveled 40 miles (64.4 kilometers) to Derbai, a frontier town.
Eliyah (Elijah) Flees from Izevel (Jezebel)
After killing Ba’al’s (Baal’s) prophets, Eliyah fled from Izevel to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba), then to the wilderness, and then to Mt Horev (Horeb) (Sinay (Sinai)).
Ezra’s Journey to Yerushalem (Jerusalem)

Ezra led a second group of exiles back to Yehudah (Judah) and Yerushalem about 80 years after the first group. He traveled the dangerous route without military escort (Ezr 8:22), but the people prayed and, under Ezra’s godly leadership, arrived safely in Yerushalem after several months.
Galatia and the Surrounding Regions

Paulos (Paul) and Barnabas, thrown out of Antiokeia (Antioch) in Pisidia, descended the mountains, going east into Lukaonia (Lycaonia). They went first to Ikonion (Iconium), a commercial center on the road between Asia and Aram (Syria). After preaching there, they had to flee to Lustra (Lystra), 25 miles (40.2 kilometers) south. Paulos was stoned in Lustra, but he and Barnabas traveled the 50 miles (80.4 kilometers) to Derbai (Derbe), a border town. The pair then boldly retraced their steps.
Gid’on’s (Gideon’s) Battle
Gid’on routed thousands of Midyanites (Midianites), chasing them to Tsererah (Zererah) and Avel-Meholah (Abel-meholah).
Illurikon (Illyricum)
According to Romans 15:19, Paulos (Paul) had preached the gospel from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to Illurikon, but at the time of writing, he had not yet gone to Romai (Rome).

item.name: ImportantPlacesinJesusMinistryinGalilee
item.title: Important Places in Jesus’ Ministry in Galilee

body.p: Important Places in Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)’ Ministry in Galil (Galilee)

After returning to his hometown, Nazaret (Nazareth), from Kafarnaoum (Capernaum), Yeshua preached in the villages of Galil and sent his disciples out to preach as well. After meeting back in Kafarnaoum, they left by boat to rest, only to be met by the crowds who followed the boat along the shore.
Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)’ Miraculous Powers Displayed
Yeshua calmed the storm on the Sea of Galil (Galilee), then cast out demons from two men in Gadara.
Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Travels toward Yerushalem (Jerusalem)
Yeshua left Galil (Galilee) for the last time, heading toward Yerushalem and death. He again crossed the Yarden (Jordan), spending some time in Perea before going on to Yeriho (Jericho).
Yonah’s (Jonah’s) Roundabout Journey
When Yonah was called to go to Nineveh, he ran from God by boarding a ship in Yafo (Joppa) headed for Tarshish in Spania (Spain). Eventually, Yonah could not hide from God; he went to Nineveh.

item.name: JonathanDefeatedtheGarrisonatGibeah
item.title: Jonathan Defeated the Garrison at Gibeah

body.p: Yonatan (Jonathan) Defeated the Garrison at Giveah (Gibeah)

Yonatan, Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) son, left the camp at Giveah and crept to the Pelishti (Philistine) camp at Mikmas (Micmash). With God’s help, Yonatan and his armor bearer surprised the Pelishtim (Philistines), who panicked and began killing each other! Sha’ul’s army heard the commotion and chased the Pelishtim as far as Beyt-Aven (Beth-aven) and Ayalon (Aijalon).

item.name: JosephandMarysJourneytoBethlehem
item.title: Joseph and Mary’s Journey to Bethlehem

body.p: Yosef (Joseph) and Maria’s (Mary’s) Journey to Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem)

Kaisar’s (Caesar’s) decree for a census of the entire Roman Empire made it necessary for Yosef and Maria to leave their hometown, Nazaret (Nazareth), and journey the 70 miles (112.6 kilometers) to the Yehudi (Judean) village of Beyt-Lehem.
Yehoshua (Joshua) Conquers Ay (Ai)

After an unsuccessful first attempt, the Israelis (Israelites) attacked Ay again and were successful. Joshu sent one detachment of soldiers to lie in wait while he led a second group against the city. When the army of Ay attacked, Yehoshua’s men occupied the enemy while the men lying in ambush moved in and burned the city.
Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) Final Days
Yehoshua gave his final speech at Shekem (Shechem), then went to his hometown, Timnat-Serah (Timnath-serah), where he died.
Yehudah (Judah) Fights for Its Land

The tribe of Yehudah wasted no time beginning their conquest of the territory allotted to them. With help from the tribe of Shim’on (Simeon), Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was conquered, as were the Kena’anim (Canaanites) in the Negev and along the coast. Hevron (Hebron) and Devir (Debir) fell to Yehudah, and later so did Azah (Gaza), Ashkelon, and Ekron.

Key Places in 1 Kings
Key Places in 1 Samuel

Key Places in 2 Samuel
Key Places in Acts

The apostle Paulos (Paul), whose missionary journeys fill much of this book, traveled tremendous distances as he tirelessly spread the gospel across much of the Roman Empire. His combined trips, by land and ship, equal more than 13,000 miles (20,917 kilometers).
Key Places in Genesis

God created the universe and the earth. Then he made man and woman, giving them a home in a beautiful garden. Unfortunately, Adam and Havah (Eve) disobeyed God and were banished from the Garden (3:23).
Key Places in Numbers
The book of Numbers begins at Mt Sinay (Sinai) and ends at the plains of Moav (Moab). From there, the Israelis (Israelites) entered the Promised Land.

item.name: KeyPlacesintheBookofJoshua
item.title: Key Places in the Book of Joshua

body.p: Key Places in the Book of Yehoshua (Joshua)
Key Places in the Exodus

The Israelis (Israelites) left Sukot (Succoth) and camped first at Etam (Etham) before going toward Ba’al-Tsefon (Baal-zephon) to camp by the sea (14:2). God miraculously brought them across the sea, into the Shur Desert (15:22). After stopping at the oasis of Eylim (Elim), the people moved into the Sin Desert (16:1).

item.name: KeyPlacesintheStoryofBalaam
item.title: Key Places in the Story of Balaam

body.p: Key Places in the Story of Bil’am (Balaam)

At King Balak’s request, Bil’am traveled nearly 400 miles (643.6 kilometers) to curse Yisrael (Israel). Balak took Bil’am to Bamot-Ba’al (Bamoth-baal) (“the high places of Ba’al (Baal)”), then to Pisgah Peak, and finally to Mt Pe’or (Peor). Each place looked over the plains of Moav (Moab), where the Israelis (Israelites) were camped. But to the king’s dismay, Bil’am blessed, not cursed, Yisrael.

item.name: KingHiramSuppliesSolomonwithBuildingMaterialsfortheTemple
item.title: King Hiram Supplies Solomon with Building Materials for the Temple

body.p: King Hiram Supplies Shelomoh (Solomon) with Building Materials for the Temple
Cedar logs were cut in Levanon (Lebanon), floated by sea to Yafo (Joppa), and then transported to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
Location of Zevulun (Zebulun)
This map shows the location of Zevulun in relation to the other tribes west of the Yarden (Jordan).
Mesopotamia: The Land between the Hidekel (Tigris) and Perat (Euphrates)
Mitulainai (Mitylene)

On his third missionary journey Paulos (Paul) stopped at Mitulainai before going on to Milaitos (Miletus). In Milaitos he summoned the elders of the Efesos (Ephesian) church to say farewell to them, because he knew he would probably not see them again.

item.name: MoabEastofthePromisedLand
item.title: Moab: East of the Promised Land

body.p: Moav (Moab): East of the Promised Land

item.name: MosesFleesfromEgypttoMidian
item.title: Moses Flees from Egypt to Midian

body.p: Mosheh (Moses) Flees from Mitsrayim (Egypt) to Midyan (Midian)
After murdering an Mitsri (Egyptian), Mosheh escaped into Midyan. There he married Tsiporah (Zipporah) and became a shepherd.

item.name: MosesLeadstheIsraelitestoMountSinai
item.title: Moses Leads the Israelites to Mount Sinai

body.p: Mosheh (Moses) Leads the Israelis (Israelites) to Mount Sinay (Sinai)

item.name: MosesLeadstheIsraelitestowardthePromisedLand
item.title: Moses Leads the Israelites toward the Promised Land

body.p: Mosheh (Moses) Leads the Israelis (Israelites) toward the Promised Land
Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah’s) Journey to Yerushalem (Jerusalem)

When Nehemyah heard that the rebuilding projects in Yerushalem were progressing slowly, he asked the king of the Medo-Persian Empire, for whom he worked, for permission to go there to help his people complete the task of rebuilding their city’s walls. The king agreed to let him go; so he left as soon as possible, traveling along much the same route Ezra had taken seven years earlier.

item.name: PatmosandtheSevenLocalChurchesinRevelation
item.title: Patmos and the Seven Local Churches in Revelation

body.p: Patmos and the Seven Local Churches in Revelation
Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) wrote to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia while he was in exile on the island of Patmos.

item.name: PaulandBarnabassMinistryinLystra
item.title: Paul and Barnabas’s Ministry in Lystra

body.p: Paulos (Paul) and Barnabas’s Ministry in Lustra (Lystra)

Paulos and Barnabas, thrown out of Antiokeia (Antioch) in Pisidia, descended the mountains, going east into Lukaonia (Lycaonia). They went first to Ikonion (Iconium), a commercial center on the road between Asia and Aram (Syria). After preaching there, they had to flee to Lustra, 25 miles (40.2 kilometers) south. Paulos was stoned in Lustra, but he and Barnabas traveled the 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) to Derbai (Derbe), a frontier town. The pair then boldly retraced their steps.

item.name: PaulandBarnabasTravelthroughPamphyliaattheEndoftheFirstMissionaryJourney
item.title: Paul and Barnabas Travel through Pamphylia at the End of the First Missionary Journey

body.p: Paulos (Paul) and Barnabas Travel through Pamfulia (Pamphylia) at the End of the First Missionary Journey
Paulos (Paul) Searches for Titos (Titus)

Paulos hoped to find Titos in Troias (Troas) and receive news about the Korinthios (Corinthian) church. Not finding him there, he went to Makedonia (Macedonia) (most likely to Filippou (Philippi)), where he found Titos.
Paulos’s (Paul’s) First Missionary Journey
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Journey to Romai (Rome)
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Return to Tarsos (Tarsus)
After time in Arav (Arabia), Paulos returned to Damesek (Damascus), then Yerushalem (Jerusalem). After troubles in Yerushalem, he fled to Kaisareia (Caesarea), then on to Tarsos.
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Second Missionary Journey
Paulos’s (Paul’s) Third Missionary Journey
Paulos (Paul) Travels to Makedonia (Macedonia)
When Paulos received the “Makedonian (Macedonian) call,” he went to Neapolis and on to Filippou (Philippi) in Makedonia.
Phoenix, Harbor Town in Kraitai (Crete)
On Paulos’s (Paul’s) journey to Romai (Rome), a storm forced the ship to bypass Phoenix on its way to Italia (Italy).

item.name: PossibleLocationofSodomandGomorrah
item.title: Possible Location of Sodom and Gomorrah

body.p: Possible Location of Sedom (Sodom) and Amorah (Gomorrah)

This map shows one possible location for Sedom and Amorah. It also shows the route Avram (Abram) took when chasing Kedorlaomer, who had conquered Sedom and taken many captives, among them Avram’s nephew Lot (Gn 14:14-16).
Refidim (Rephidim)
The map shows the possible location of Refidim. Here God supplied water from a rock for the Israelis (Israelites).
Raigion (Rhegium)
Paulos (Paul) stopped by the Italia (Italian) harbor of Raigion on his way to Romai (Rome).

item.name: SennacheribLeadsHisTroopsfromNinevehtowardIsrael
item.title: Sennacherib Leads His Troops from Nineveh toward Israel

body.p: Sanheriv (Sennacherib) Leads His Troops from Nineveh toward Yisrael (Israel)
Shekem (Shechem)
Avram’s (Abram’s) journey from Ur to Shekem
Shipwrecked at Melitai (Malta)

Paulos (Paul) began his 2,000-mile (3,218-kilometer) trip to Romai (Rome) at Kaisareia (Caesarea). To avoid the open seas, the ship followed the coastline. At Mura (Myra), Paulos was put on a vessel bound for Italia (Italy). It arrived with difficulty at Knidos (Cnidus), then went to Kraitai (Crete), landing at the port of Fair Havens. The next stop was Phoenix, but the ship was blown south around the island of Klaudai (Cauda), then drifted for two weeks until it was shipwrecked on the island of Melitai.
Sukar (Sychar) in Shomron (Samaria)
Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) passed through Sukar on his way to various towns in Galil (Galilee).
Surakousai (Syracuse)
Paulos (Paul) traveled from Melitai (Malta) to Surakousai on his way to Romai (Rome).
The Battle for Giveon (Gibeon)
Yisrael (Israel) attacked the Amori (Amorite) kings outside of Giveon and chased them as far as Makedah (Makkedah).

item.name: TheBeginningofPaulandBarnabassFirstJourney
item.title: The Beginning of Paul and Barnabas’s First Journey

body.p: Salamis
This city on the Mediterranean island of Kupros (Cyprus) was the first stop for Paulos (Paul), Barnabas, and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (Mark) on the first missionary journey.

item.name: TheChurchesofPetersFirstLetter
item.title: The Churches of Peter’s First Letter

body.p: The Churches of Kefa’s (Peter’s; Grk. Petros’) First Letter

Kefa addressed his letter to the churches located throughtout Bithunia (Bithynia), Pontos (Pontus), Asia, Galatia, and Kappadokia (Cappadocia). Paulos (Paul) had evangelized many of these areas; other areas had churches that were begun by the Yehudim (Jews) who were in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) on the day of Pentecost and heard Kefa’s powerful sermon (see Acts 2:9-11).
The Conquered Land

Yehoshua (Joshua) displayed brilliant military strategy in the way he went about conquering the land of Kena’an (Canaan). He first captured the well-fortified city of Yeriho (Jericho) to gain a foothold in Kena’an and to demonstrate the awesome might of the God of Yisrael (Israel). Then he gained the hill country around Beyt-El (Bethel) and Giveon (Gibeon). From there he subdued towns in the lowlands. Then his army conquered important cities in the north, such as Hatsor (Hazor). In all, Yisrael conquered land both east and west of the Yarden (Jordan) River, from Mt Hermon in the north to beyond the Negev to Mt Halak in the south.
The Death of Mosheh (Moses)
Not allowed to enter the Promised Land, Mosheh climbed Mt Nevo (Nebo) to look at it just before his death.
The Divided Kingdom

Rehav’am’s (Rehoboam’s) threat of heavier burdens caused a rebellion and divided the nation. Rehav’am ruled the southern kingdom; Yarov’am (Jeroboam) ruled the northern kingdom. Yarov’am set up idols in Dan and Beyt-El (Bethel) to discourage worship in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). At the same time, Aram, Amon (Ammon), Moav (Moab), and Edom claimed independence from the divided nation.

item.name: TheFirstMissionaryJourneytoCyprus
item.title: The First Missionary Journey: To Cyprus

body.p: The First Missionary Journey: To Kupros (Cyprus)

The leaders of the church in Antiokeia (Antioch) chose Paulos (Paul) and Barnabas to take the gospel westward. Along with Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (Mark), they boarded ship at Seleukeia (Seleucia) and set out across the Mediterranean for Kupros. They preached in Salamis, the largest city, and went across the island to Pafos (Paphos).
The Garden of Gethsaimanai (Gethsemane)
After the Last Supper, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) went to Gethsaimanai, where he was arrested and taken to Kayafa’s (Caiaphas’; Grk. Kaiafas’) house.

item.name: TheIsraelitesWanderintheWilderness
item.title: The Israelites Wander in the Wilderness

body.p: The Israelis (Israelites) Wander in the Wilderness
The Last Evening

After Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) singled Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) out for arrest, the mob took Yeshua first to Hanan (Annas; Grk. Hannas) and then to Kayafa (Caiaphas; Grk. Kaiafas), the high priest. This trial, a mockery of justice, convened at daybreak and ended with their decision to kill him, but the Yehudim (Jews) needed Romai’s (Rome’s) permission for the death sentence. Yeshua was taken to Pilatos (Pilate) (who was probably in the Praetorium), then to Herodes (Herod) (Lk 23:5-12), and back to Pilatos, who sentenced him to die.
The Medo-Persian Empire

The Medo-Persian Empire included the lands of Media and Paras (Persia), much of the area shown on this map and more. The Jewish exiles were concentrated in the area around Nippur in the Babylonian province. The decree by King Koresh (Cyrus) that allowed the Israelis (Israelites) to return to their homeland and rebuild the temple was discovered in the palace at Ahmeta (Ecbatana).
The Seven Churches of Revelation

The seven churches were located on a major Roman road. A letter carrier would leave the island of Patmos (where Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) was exiled), arriving first at Efesos (Ephesus). He would travel north to Smurna (Smyrna) and Pergamos (Pergamum), turn southeast to Thuateira (Thyatira), and continue on to Sardeis (Sardis), Filadelfeia (Philadelphia), and Laodikeia (Laodicea)—in the exact order in which the letters were dictated.
The Showdown at Karmel (Carmel)

In a showdown with the false prophets of Ba’al (Baal) at Mt Karmel, Eliyah (Elijah) set out to prove to Ahav (Ahab) that only the Lord is God. Eliyah then killed the false prophets in the Kishon Valley and fled back to Yizre’el (Jezreel).
The Story of Ruth
Elimelek (Elimelech), No’omi (Naomi), and their two sons went to the land of Moav (Moab). No’omi returned to Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) after her husband and sons died.

item.name: TheTribesEastoftheJordan
item.title: The Tribes East of the Jordan

body.p: The Tribes East of the Yarden (Jordan)

Yehoshua (Joshua) assigned territory to the tribes of Re’uven (Reuben), Gad, and the half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh) on the east side of the Yarden. These tribes had asked Mosheh (Moses) for land there because it was such wonderful livestock country (Nm 32:1-5).

item.name: TheTribesWestoftheJordan
item.title: The Tribes West of the Jordan

body.p: The Tribes West of the Yarden (Jordan)

Yehudah (Judah), Efrayim (Ephraim), and the other half-tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh) were the first tribes to receive land west of the Yarden. The remaining seven tribes—Benyamin (Benjamin), Zevulun (Zebulun), Yisakar (Issachar), Asher, Naftali (Naphtali), Shim’on (Simeon), and Dan—received their inheritance later because they were slow to conquer and possess the land allotted to them.

item.name: TitusServestheChurchesinCrete
item.title: Titus Serves the Churches in Crete

body.p: Titos (Titus) Serves the Churches in Kraitai (Crete)

Tradition says that after Paulos (Paul) was released from prison in Romai (Rome) (before his second and final Roman imprisonment), he and Titos traveled together for a while. They stopped in Kraitai, and when it was time for Paulos to go, he left Titos behind to help the churches there.
Two Possible Sites for Golgotha

This map shows the boundaries of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) day. Two possible sites for Golgotha (meaning “the place of the skull”) are shown—one to the north of the city, outside the Fish Gate; and one to the west of the city, nearer to Herodes’s (Herod’s) palace.
Ur of the Kasdim (Chaldeans)
Valley of Eschol
The spies traveled from Kadesh-Barnea (Kadesh-barnea), through the valley of Eshkol (Eshcol), to Rehov (Rehob), and back again—a total of 500 miles (804.5 kilometers).
